profile.products: VNC image (vnc/), WASM image with save server (wasm/server.go), Go remake (remake/)
profile.api: internal save API of the WASM image (GET/PUT /api/saves/{name})
profile.assessed_branch: remake at a2f21af plus the uncommitted harness-build changes (--worktree); default branch is main

results.name: Formatter
results.why: Style churn disappears from diffs and the agent matches house style for free.
results.passes_when: an auto-formatter is configured in the repo.

results.name: Lint Config
results.why: The agent sees its own mistakes in seconds instead of in review.
results.passes_when: a linter configuration for the language of the main application code is committed; a linter that only covers other files (Markdown, YAML, skill files) does not count.

evidence.detail: lint task over remake/ and wasm/

results.name: Strict Typing
results.why: Strict types reject plausible-but-wrong edits before they run.
results.passes_when: the strictest common type setting is on.

results.name: Type Check
results.why: Types are the cheapest correctness signal an agent can verify itself.
results.passes_when: the code is statically typed or a type checker is configured.

evidence.detail: Go is statically typed and compiled

results.name: Large File Detection
results.why: Small files fit the agent's context and stay quick to read.
results.passes_when: something stops oversized files from landing.

evidence.detail: no .gitattributes, no size check in .githooks/pre-commit or ci.yml

results.fix: Add a size check for new files (a few lines in .githooks/pre-commit and CI), with an allowlist for the original game files in bmp/ and remake/internal/embedded/data.

results.name: Naming Consistency
results.why: Predictable names let the agent find code and guess intent.
results.passes_when: naming conventions are written down (agent guide, CONTRIBUTING, style guide) or enforced by lint rules (pep8-naming, ESLint naming-convention, Checkstyle), and a sample of three modules follows them. Consistent but undocumented, unenforced naming fails.

evidence.detail: the save server does not follow it yet

results.fix: Rename the German identifiers in wasm/server.go (immerNachfragen, dateien) to English and enforce Go naming with revive in .golangci.yml.

results.name: Pre-commit Hooks
results.why: Mistakes surface at commit time, while the change is still fresh.
results.passes_when: a commit-time hook framework is configured.

results.name: Code Modularization
results.why: Enforced boundaries keep each agent edit inside one module.
results.passes_when: module or layer boundaries are enforced by a tool.

evidence.detail: Go internal/ packages: assets, game, ui, embedded

results.name: Cyclomatic Complexity
results.why: Small functions are ones an agent can change safely.
results.passes_when: a complexity limit is configured.
results.fix: Enable gocyclo or gocognit in the golangci-lint config with a threshold at today's maximum and lower it over time.

results.name: Dead Code Detection
results.why: Without dead paths, the agent spends its effort only on code that runs.
results.passes_when: a dedicated dead-code tool runs in CI over the main application code. Lint rules for unused imports or variables alone do not count.

evidence.detail: CI runs vet, gofmt and tests only

results.fix: Run golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode (or golangci-lint unused) in the CI remake job.

results.name: Duplicate Code Detection
results.why: Each behaviour lives in one place, so the agent changes it once.
results.passes_when: duplicate-code detection runs in CI.
results.fix: Enable the dupl linter in golangci-lint with a sensible threshold.

results.name: Tech Debt Tracking
results.why: Linked TODOs give the agent a readable list of known gaps.
results.passes_when: debt markers follow a machine-readable convention that links to a ticket, enforced by a lint rule or scanner. Without such a rule the criterion fails, even if the code has no TODOs today.
results.fix: Require an issue reference on TODO/FIXME via the godox linter in golangci-lint (today the Go code has no TODOs, so it passes at once).

results.name: N+1 Detection
results.why: N+1 queries an agent introduces are caught before they reach production.
results.passes_when: N+1 queries in the main application code are caught automatically: query-count assertions in tests, an N+1 detector, or ORM settings that raise on lazy loading (`raise_on_sql`, `strict_loading`).

results.name: Dependencies Pinned
results.why: The agent, the team, and CI resolve the same versions.
results.passes_when: a lockfile pins exact dependency versions and is committed.

results.name: Toolchain Pinned
results.why: The agent, the team, and CI run the same runtime versions, so every failure the agent sees is one everyone can reproduce.
results.passes_when: the runtime of the main application code (Node, Python, JDK, .NET SDK, Go …) and its package manager are pinned in a committed file that local setup and CI both read. A CI step that installs either of them unpinned fails the criterion; pinning further tools is welcome but not required.

evidence.detail: golangci-lint pinned, installed by mise-action in CI

results.name: Documented Build Commands
results.why: With the canonical command written down, the agent can verify its own work.
results.passes_when: build and run commands are written in the README, CONTRIBUTING, or the agent guide, or in an in-repo doc one link away from them.

results.name: Git Hosting CLI
results.why: The agent can open PRs and read CI results without a browser.
results.passes_when: scripts or docs for working on this repo use a scriptable hosting CLI; a mention in product content does not count.

evidence.detail: gh for pull requests and CI results

results.name: Single Command Setup
results.why: One setup command gets the agent past the step where it most often gets stuck.
results.passes_when: one documented command takes a fresh clone, with its stated prerequisites installed (Docker, mise …), to a state where the tests run. A script that chains several steps counts; several commands listed in the docs do not. A devcontainer counts only when the docs present it as the complete setup path. If the tests need gitignored files (a local config, test data), the setup or the agent tool's environment setup provides them, so a fresh agent worktree gets there too.

evidence.detail: prerequisites: Go, mise, Linux GL/X11 headers
mise run remake:test runs from a fresh clone; go fetches modules, test data is committed

results.name: Check Command
results.why: One command after every change is the agent's tightest feedback loop and tells it exactly which checks matter.
results.passes_when: a single documented command runs all fast checks (format, lint, types, unit tests), is named in the agent guide, and stops with a non-zero exit code on the first failure (a task runner target, a script with `set -e`, or a build tool goal).

results.name: Agentic Development
results.why: Existing agent config and skills are something to build on.
results.passes_when: the repo shows traces of working with agents: a committed configuration or instruction file of an agent tool, agent skills or commands, or agent co-author trailers in the history.

results.name: Automated PR Review
results.why: Agent-written PRs get a consistent first pass before a human.
results.passes_when: pull requests get an automated first-pass review: feedback on the code change, from an AI reviewer or a bot with rules on the diff (Danger, Reviewdog), and the project-specific review rules it applies are versioned in the repo. A generic AI reviewer without the project's rules fails: it does not know what this project gets wrong. Checks of the template, labels, or title alone do not count.

evidence.detail: ci.yml and release.yml only; no reviewer, no review rules

results.fix: Run an AI or rule-based reviewer on pull requests fed by a committed REVIEW.md (for example the claude-code-action with the project's review rules).

results.name: Fast CI Feedback
results.why: Short CI keeps the agent's edit-verify loop tight.
results.passes_when: CI runs on pull/merge requests and runs the same checks as the documented check command (or, without one, the documented lint, type, and test commands), ideally by calling it, so local and CI results cannot drift apart.

results.name: Feature Flag Infrastructure
results.why: Agent changes can ship dark instead of all-or-nothing.
results.passes_when: a flag system switches behaviour at runtime per environment, tenant, or user (a flag SDK, OpenFeature, or a flag module with targeting). Plain config booleans or `*_ENABLED` variables do not count.
results.fix: Introduce a small flag mechanism (OpenFeature or a flag file read at start) for behaviour that should ship dark, or waive this for a single-user game.

results.name: Release Automation
results.why: An automated release is one the agent can carry through to the end.
results.passes_when: CI publishes versioned releases (tags, versioned packages or images, release entries). Continuous deployment without versions counts for `deployment_frequency`, not here.

evidence.detail: versioned tags, images and GitHub releases

results.name: Infrastructure as Code
results.why: Infrastructure the agent can read and validate is infrastructure it can change, and the plan shows reviewers what the change will do before anything is applied.
results.passes_when: the infrastructure the team runs is defined as code in this repo or one the agent guide links, and every change to it is validated before merge: format, validate, and lint locally or in CI, and the plan or diff against the target environment shows on the pull/merge request. Infrastructure set up by hand in a console fails.

evidence.detail: the operated setup is defined as compose
no validation of the compose files

results.fix: Validate both compose files in CI (`docker compose -f vnc/docker-compose.yml config`, same for wasm) and show the image/compose diff on the pull request.

results.name: Generated Code Marked
results.why: A hand edit to generated code is lost on the next generator run; the agent avoids it only when it can tell generated files apart and CI catches drift.
results.passes_when: committed generator output (API clients, contract types, catalogs, lockstep copies) is recognisable as such, by a header, `linguist-generated` in `.gitattributes`, or a list in the agent guide naming the generator command, and CI regenerates it and fails when the result differs from what is committed. Large generated or vendored trees the agent has no reason to read are kept out of its search, by `.gitignore` or a deny rule in the shared agent tool configuration.
results.fix: Mark remake/internal/embedded/data as linguist-generated in .gitattributes and deny it in a shared .claude/settings.json; AGENTS.md already names remake:extract.

results.name: Build Performance Tracking
results.why: Tracked build times keep every agent loop fast as the codebase grows.
results.passes_when: builds are cached or their timing is visible.

results.name: Agent Outcome Tracking
results.why: Whether agents help shows in the numbers: lead time, rework, human interventions.
results.passes_when: the team regularly collects at least two measures of agent contributions (share of agent pull requests, revert or rework rate, review rounds per pull request, lead time) and keeps them in the repo or links them from it.
results.fix: Mark agent commits (see agent_change_traceability) and add a small script that reports agent share and reverts from git log.

results.name: Deployment Frequency
results.why: Small, frequent deploys match the size of agent changes.
results.passes_when: deployments run automatically and regularly.
results.fix: Release automatically (for example on every push to main that passes CI, or on a schedule) instead of only by manual dispatch; Watchtower then deploys.

results.name: Post-Deploy Verification
results.why: A smoke suite against the deployed environment tells the agent whether its change works where it runs, not just in tests.
results.passes_when: after every automated deployment a smoke or synthetic test suite runs against that environment, and a failure stops promotion to the next stage (test → integration → production) or triggers a rollback. Health checks alone do not count.

evidence.detail: Watchtower pulls new images, nothing verifies them

results.fix: After Watchtower updates the NAS container, run the smoke/bench check against it (a small scheduled job or a Watchtower post-update hook) and roll back on failure.

results.name: Release Notes Automation
results.why: Generated notes give commits a format the agent can follow.
results.passes_when: release notes are generated.

results.name: Unused Dependencies Detection
results.why: A lean dependency graph is less for the agent to understand.
results.passes_when: unused dependencies are detected in CI.

evidence.detail: all requirements marked // indirect, so go.mod is not tidy

results.fix: Add a CI step `go mod tidy && git diff --exit-code go.mod go.sum` in remake/; it would already flag that every requirement in go.mod is marked // indirect.

results.name: Dead Feature Flag Detection
results.why: Removing stale flags keeps every branch the agent reads a live one.
results.passes_when: stale feature flags are detected automatically.

results.name: Heavy Dependency Detection
results.why: Size budgets keep the code lean when an agent reaches for a library to save a few lines.
results.passes_when: shipped bundles have size budgets.

evidence.detail: static pages; js-dos is loaded from a CDN (wasm/index.html:42), no bundler

results.name: Monorepo Tooling
results.why: The task graph shows the agent what a change affects across packages.
results.passes_when: the monorepo uses workspace-aware build tooling. A system split over several repos passes when a committed workspace manifest lets the agent check out and update all of them with one command.

evidence.detail: check spans remake and the save server, not the images

results.fix: Let `mise run check` (or a `check:all`) also depend on wasm:smoke and vnc:bench so one task graph spans all three products.

results.name: Progressive Rollout
results.why: A regression an agent introduced reaches few users first.
results.passes_when: deployments roll out progressively.

evidence.detail: latest moves for every host at once

results.fix: Release to a canary tag first (for example `next`) that one instance follows before `latest` moves, or waive this for a single-host deployment.

results.name: Rollback Automation
results.why: Cheap rollback makes shipping agent changes low-risk.
results.passes_when: rollback is one command or automatic.
results.fix: Add a workflow (or mise task) that moves `latest`/`wasm` back to a given earlier version with `docker buildx imagetools create`, and document it.

results.name: Version Drift Detection
results.why: One version per dependency across packages keeps agent changes compatible.
results.passes_when: shared dependency versions are kept aligned across packages.
results.fix: Check in CI that the golang image of wasm/Dockerfile matches go.mod (one line of shell).

results.name: Unit Tests Exist
results.why: Tests are the strongest signal an agent can check its change against.
results.passes_when: unit tests exist in the stack's standard layout.

evidence.detail: remake: unit tests in assets, game, ui
the VNC image has no code of its own beyond the start script of a third-party emulator, covered by the bench

results.name: Test Naming Conventions
results.why: The agent finds and extends the right tests by convention.
results.passes_when: test names and placement are consistent across the suite.

evidence.detail: *_test.go next to the code, Test<Behaviour> names

results.name: Unit Tests Runnable
results.why: Tests the agent can run itself let it verify every change.
results.passes_when: one documented command runs the unit tests; in a repo with several products, one command per product is enough.

evidence.detail: mise run check runs all unit tests

results.name: Test Stage Rules
results.why: Named test stages tell the agent when to run the slower suites, so CI confirms its work instead of surprising it.
results.passes_when: for every check outside the fast checks (the check command, or without one the documented lint, type, and unit test commands), such as integration, end-to-end, contract, or performance suites, the agent guide says when it is required, for example "end-to-end tests when routes or the UI change".

evidence.detail: vnc:bench, wasm:smoke and screen comparison with the change that requires them

results.name: Integration Tests Exist
results.why: They catch the cross-module breakage unit tests miss.
results.passes_when: integration or end-to-end tests cover real flows.

evidence.detail: Playwright run against the VNC image with --check
page, bundle and save API of the WASM image

results.name: Test Isolation
results.why: Isolated tests give the agent pass/fail signals it can trust.
results.passes_when: the main unit suite runs in parallel (configured, or the framework's default as in Go or Vitest) without shared mutable fixtures. A parallel end-to-end suite alone does not count.

evidence.detail: go test runs packages in parallel by default
each test gets its own temporary data directory

results.name: Flaky Test Detection
results.why: Stable tests keep red meaningful, so the agent takes every failure seriously.
results.passes_when: flaky tests are recorded where people can see them over time: a quarantine list, a flaky-test report or dashboard, retry telemetry, or a tracking label. Retries alone do not count.
results.fix: Record failed-then-passed CI runs (for example a weekly job running `go test -count=3` that files an issue on a flaky test).

results.name: Test Coverage Thresholds
results.why: A gate pushes the agent to test what it changes.
results.passes_when: coverage is measured in CI and published or gated by a threshold. A coverage configuration that only runs locally does not count.
results.fix: Run `go test -coverprofile` in the check, publish it in CI and fail below the measured value.

results.name: Mutation Testing
results.why: Coverage shows the code ran, not that a test would notice it breaking; mutation testing catches the assertion-free tests an agent writes to turn a gate green.
results.passes_when: mutation testing runs in CI over the main application code, in full or on the changed code, and its score is published or gated. A run that only happens locally does not count.
results.fix: Run a Go mutation tester (for example go-mutesting or gremlins) on changed packages in a CI job and publish the score.

results.name: Test Performance Tracking
results.why: Tracked test times keep the suite and the agent's loop fast.
results.passes_when: test suite timing is tracked over time.
results.fix: Upload `go test -json` timings from CI (or `gotestsum --junitfile`) and watch the slowest tests.

results.name: Gate Ratchet
results.why: Gates that only tighten keep "green" meaningful, even when weakening a test would be the agent's quickest way out.
results.passes_when: weakening a gate is visible: coverage floors only rise (a ratchet, or per-module floors at the measured value), skip and ignore markers need a reference (enforced by lint), and a change to test, lint, or CI configuration cannot land without owner review that the platform enforces: CODEOWNERS with code-owner approval required on the default branch (GitHub branch protection or a ruleset; GitLab Premium or higher), a path-based required-reviewer policy in Azure DevOps, or GitLab approval rules, while nobody pushes to the default branch directly, since a direct push skips the review. Where the platform cannot enforce owner review (GitLab Free, direct pushes), a CI check that fails when a gate is weaker than on the base commit does the same. A CODEOWNERS file alone does not count.
results.fix: Add CODEOWNERS entries for .golangci.yml, mise.toml, .github/ and *_test.go, require code-owner review on main, and pin a coverage floor.

results.name: README
results.why: It is the agent's first orientation in the repo.
results.passes_when: the root README says what the project is, how to set it up and run it (or that there is nothing to build), and where the main parts live, directly or by linking docs inside the repo. A README that only links to an external website fails; a link to the rendered site of docs kept in this repo counts as a doc inside the repo when the evidence names their source folder.

evidence.detail: layout with remake/, docs and AGENTS.md

results.name: Agent Guide
results.why: An agent guide is the single most effective readiness artifact.
results.passes_when: an agent guide exists. Presence only; the next criteria grade content.

results.name: Agent Guide Substance
results.why: A guide with substance but no bulk teaches the agent the essentials and leaves room for the code.
results.passes_when: the guide is more than a stub and still fits comfortably in context (roughly 20 to 300 lines, a guideline from 2026 context sizes; encyclopedic parts are linked out).

results.name: Documentation Freshness
results.why: Current docs lead the agent along paths that still exist.
results.passes_when: the newest commit touching any core doc (README, CONTRIBUTING, agent guide, `docs/`) is at most 180 days older than the repo's latest commit.

evidence.detail: 2026-10-23, same day as the latest commit

results.name: Agent Guide Completeness
results.why: A guide that names the test command lets the agent verify every change.
results.passes_when: the guide covers the test command, build/run commands, repo layout, the architecture style when the code follows one (hexagonal, layered …), conventions, and which docs to update with which kind of change (a definition of done); it leaves out what code and config already state, and nothing in it is contradicted by the configuration (for example a strict mode the config does not enable).

results.name: Agent Guide Freshness
results.why: Agents trust the guide, and a current guide earns that trust.
results.passes_when: the agent guide was changed within about six months of the repo's latest commit.

results.name: Agent Boundaries
results.why: What an agent may not decide alone it has to know before it acts, not after.
results.passes_when: the agent guide names what an agent does not change without asking (for example public interfaces, database migrations, dependencies, security configuration) and when it stops and asks (escalation rules). This is the stated intent; `agent_action_guardrails` grades whether the tool configuration enforces it.

evidence.detail: ask before releases, CI changes, dependencies, bmp/; stop when spec and decompilation disagree

results.name: Scoped Agent Guides
results.why: In a large repo the context belongs where the work happens; one guide for everything grows too long or too vague.
results.passes_when: each subproject or main module has its own short agent guide covering only its area, with test and lint commands scoped to it (running the whole suite after a change to one subproject costs time and context), and the root guide points to them.
results.fix: Give wasm/ and vnc/ a short scoped guide each (build, smoke/bench command, ports) and link them from AGENTS.md; remake/CLAUDE.md is one already.

results.name: API Schema Docs
results.why: A machine-readable schema lets the agent call APIs correctly.
results.passes_when: machine-readable API schemas are committed or generated.

evidence.detail: save API registered without a schema

results.fix: Commit a short OpenAPI file for /api/saves/{name} (GET/PUT, name pattern, 4 MB limit, status codes) next to wasm/server.go.

results.name: Automated Doc Generation
results.why: Generated docs cannot drift, so the agent can trust them.
results.passes_when: reference docs are generated from source in a pipeline.

evidence.detail: go doc -all of the remake packages uploaded as remake-godoc

results.name: Service Flow Documented
results.why: Flows give the cross-service picture code alone does not.
results.passes_when: architecture or service flows are documented, ideally as diagrams.

evidence.detail: architecture diagram of the VNC image

results.name: Target Architecture
results.why: Agents copy what they find in the code; in grown code that is often a pattern nobody wants any more.
results.passes_when: the target architecture and the known deviations of the current code from it are documented: which patterns or modules are deprecated and what to use instead. The agent guide links to it directly or through a doc it links. A diagram of today's flows alone is `service_flow_documented`.

evidence.detail: The code follows one style throughout, with no legacy patterns to avoid.

results.name: Domain Docs
results.why: Domain language and past decisions let the agent build solutions that fit the whole system, not just the file in front of it.
results.passes_when: a glossary of domain terms and architecture decision records live in the repo, and the agent guide links to them directly or through a doc it links.

results.name: Skills
results.why: Skills turn repeated workflows into something the agent runs the same way every time.
results.passes_when: agent skills or commands with frontmatter for working on this repo exist in a folder the agent tool loads; skills the repo ships as its product (for example under `plugins/`) do not count.

results.name: Agent Rules Enforced
results.why: A rule enforced by a hook, linter, or CI check holds every time, even when an agent skips an instruction in the guide.
results.passes_when: the rules the agent guide states as mandatory (run the check command, forbidden commands, version pinning, protected paths, required documentation updates) are each backed by a hook, lint rule, or CI check; rules that cannot be checked are the exception and say so.
results.fix: Back the hard limits with .claude/settings.json: ask before `mise run release`, `gh workflow run`, `git push` to main and `podman push`; a Stop hook that runs `mise run check`.

results.name: Agent Guide Structure
results.why: Sections let the agent jump to what it needs.
results.passes_when: the guide is split into clearly headed sections.

evidence.detail: sections: Verify your work, Working with the platform, Definition of done, Conventions, Hard limits, Where to find context

results.name: Env Template
results.why: A complete template makes every required variable visible at setup.
results.passes_when: a committed template documents every required environment variable.

evidence.detail: BMP_DATA documented; the only variable the application code reads (remake/cmd/bmp/main.go:92)

results.name: Database Schema
results.why: A declared schema lets the agent reason about data and migrations.
results.passes_when: the schema is managed by migrations or a schema tool.

results.name: Local Services Setup
results.why: The agent can run the app end to end.
results.passes_when: local dependencies start with one command.

evidence.detail: no external services; remake runs standalone, the images are self-contained

results.name: Reproducible Test Data
results.why: An agent can only verify what it can run against known data.
results.passes_when: the data for local and integration tests is created by a documented command or versioned in the repo (seeds, fixtures, factories, anonymised dumps), and no test suite needs a shared or production database. `local_services_setup` grades whether the services start, this criterion what they hold.

evidence.detail: tests run against the committed original files

results.name: Devcontainer
results.why: A known-good workspace removes environment guesswork.
results.passes_when: a devcontainer configuration exists.
results.fix: Add .devcontainer/devcontainer.json with Go, mise and the GL/X11 headers plus xvfb.

results.name: Agent App Verification
results.why: An agent that can start the application and use it like a user verifies behaviour, not just tests.
results.passes_when: the docs for working on this repo say how to start the application locally, and the agent has a way to exercise it: for a web UI, browser automation set up in the agent tool configuration or documented for the agent (Playwright, a browser MCP server or CLI); for an API, documented example calls (`.http` files, a collection, curl lines); for a CLI, documented invocations.

evidence.detail: remake:shot with input scripts to drive and screenshot screens

results.name: Symbol Navigation
results.why: In a large or multi-language codebase, text search for a common name returns thousands of matches; navigation by symbol finds the one definition and its real references.
results.passes_when: the shared agent tool configuration gives the agent symbol-level navigation (go to definition, find references) for each language of the main application code, through a language server or a code intelligence tool, and the setup command or the agent guide installs what it needs.

evidence.detail: Go is the one main language, 121 .go files (< 500)

results.name: Devcontainer Runnable
results.why: A devcontainer that starts gives the agent a working environment in one step.
results.passes_when: the devcontainer declares something runnable: `image`, `build`, `dockerFile`, or `dockerComposeFile`. Declaration only; nothing is built.

results.name: Parallel Workspaces
results.why: Several agents working side by side need workspaces that start fast and do not step on each other's ports, databases, or containers.
results.passes_when: a fresh worktree reaches a state where the tests run with one documented, fast command that reuses caches and installed dependencies, several worktrees can run their tests at the same time (no fixed ports, per-worktree database or container project names), and the agent guide says to work in a worktree of its own.
results.fix: Say in AGENTS.md that agents work in their own worktree (remake/CLAUDE.md does for screens), and derive the container name and ports of vnc:run/wasm:run-docker from the worktree.

results.name: Health Checks
results.why: A definitive is-it-up signal after a change.
results.passes_when: services expose a liveness and a readiness endpoint; one endpoint that also checks required dependencies counts for both. Liveness alone fails.
results.fix: Add a readiness check that also checks dependencies: for WASM a /healthz that writes and removes a probe in /data, for VNC one that checks Xvnc and DOSBox run; point HEALTHCHECK at it.

results.name: Metrics Collection
results.why: The agent can confirm the runtime effect of a change.
results.passes_when: runtime metrics are collected.
results.fix: Expose a few Prometheus metrics from wasm/server.go (saves written, errors, request durations), or waive for a home deployment.

results.name: Structured Logging
results.why: Parseable logs are evidence the agent can debug from.
results.passes_when: a structured logging library is in use.

results.name: Alerting Configured
results.why: Regressions after a merge get noticed while the change is still fresh.
results.passes_when: alert rules live under version control.
results.fix: Define an alert on the container health (Synology notifications or an Uptime Kuma monitor) as code in the repo, or waive.

results.name: Deployment Observability
results.why: Ties a change to what happened when it rolled out.
results.passes_when: each deployment leaves a marker in monitoring: an annotation, a deploy event, or a release in the error tracker. Deploy logs that exist only in the CI system do not count.
results.fix: Have the release workflow (or Watchtower notifications) record each deploy in whatever monitoring is used.

results.name: Distributed Tracing
results.why: The agent can follow a request across services.
results.passes_when: requests are traced across services.
results.fix: Add a request ID to the logs of wasm/server.go (full OpenTelemetry is overkill here), or waive.

results.name: Error Tracking
results.why: Contextual errors point straight at the failing path.
results.passes_when: errors are tracked with context.
results.fix: Report server errors with the release version (Sentry or similar), or waive.

results.name: Profiling Instrumentation
results.why: Performance problems become diagnosable, not just correctness.
results.passes_when: a profiler can be attached to the running service: a continuous profiler, a profiling endpoint, or JFR/async-profiler configured for deployment. A debugger port alone does not count.
results.fix: Register net/http/pprof on a local-only port in wasm/server.go.

results.name: Circuit Breakers
results.why: A failure an agent change causes stays contained instead of cascading.
results.passes_when: outbound calls of the main application code use a resilience library or explicitly configured timeouts plus retries with backoff. Library defaults nobody configured do not count.

evidence.detail: no outbound calls in the Go code

results.name: Code Quality Metrics
results.why: Trends show that agent work keeps the codebase healthy, or when it starts not to.
results.passes_when: code quality trends are tracked.
results.fix: Upload `go test -coverprofile` results per pull request (Codecov or a job summary).

results.name: Runbooks Documented
results.why: The human playbook for incidents, readable by the agent too.
results.passes_when: runbooks cover incidents: how to diagnose, restart, or roll back. Development how-tos and agent skills count only where they cover incidents.

evidence.detail: troubleshooting for one case, no restart or rollback steps

results.fix: Write a short RUNBOOK.md: container unhealthy, saves fail, roll back to the previous image; the save-permission section of the README is a start.

results.name: Comprehensive .gitignore
results.why: Secrets and build noise stay out of what the agent commits.
results.passes_when: `.gitignore` excludes secrets (`.env*`), build output, and editor files.

results.name: Branch Protection
results.why: Every agent change reaches main through review.
results.passes_when: changes reach the default branch only through pull/merge requests with at least one human approval. Check practice too: most of the last 40 first-parent commits on the default branch should be pull/merge request merges. A practice without pull/merge requests is a `fail` even when the setting cannot be read; a practice with them is no proof of the rule, so without the setting or a human statement the result is `not_assessable`.

evidence.detail: 1 merge, 0 pull-request commits in the last 40

results.fix: Protect main with a ruleset: pull requests required, CI checks required (one approval for outside contributors; as sole maintainer you may allow yourself to bypass).

results.name: CODEOWNERS
results.why: Routes each change to the people who must review it.
results.passes_when: a CODEOWNERS file maps paths to owners; on Azure Repos, which has no CODEOWNERS file, a required-reviewer policy on paths does the same.

results.name: Secrets Management
results.why: Credentials stay out of the code the agent reads and writes.
results.passes_when: no credentials are committed and code reads secrets from the environment or a secret manager. Committed secret files pass only when encrypted with keys managed outside the repo; password-protected vaults or archives committed to the repo fail.

evidence.detail: Docker Hub credentials from GitHub secrets

results.name: Agent Usage Agreement
results.why: Which agent tools may see which code and data is settled with the client before the agent acts.
results.passes_when: a document in the repo, or one the agent guide links to, records which agent tools and models are allowed and which data they may see. A human statement naming where the agreement lives (a contract, the client's AI policy) also counts. In a public open-source repo, a contribution policy that says which agent use is allowed is enough; the data question does not arise. A record that still holds placeholders fails (fix: fill them in); `not_assessable` is only for a record that may exist outside the repo and no one could point to.

evidence.detail: Nothing is written down about which agent tools may be used.

results.fix: Add a short note on agent use (allowed tools, whether agent-made contributions are welcome) to the README or a CONTRIBUTING.md and link it from AGENTS.md.

results.name: Agent Setup Owner
results.why: Without an owner, the agent setup drifts into what each developer happens to know, and nobody removes what no longer helps.
results.passes_when: a named person or team owns the agent setup (agent guide, shared agent tool configuration, approved skills and plugins) and must review changes to it: CODEOWNERS entries for those paths, or the agent guide or agreement record naming the owner.

results.name: Agent Secret Access
results.why: Secrets out of the agent's reach stay out of its context, its logs, and its output.
results.passes_when: the agent tool configuration denies reading every secret-bearing file in the repo (`.env*`, token and key files, files helper scripts write tokens to), and the gap deny rules leave (commands that open files indirectly) is closed by a sandbox or by keeping tokens off the disk.
results.fix: Commit .claude/settings.json denying Read of .env*, *.pem, *.key and similar, and enable the sandbox.

results.name: Agent Action Guardrails
results.why: What the agent may do is decided beforehand, not at the moment of execution.
results.passes_when: the agent tool configuration requires approval for destructive and production-facing commands (force push, deploy, infrastructure apply, database migrations against shared environments), and no production credentials are reachable from the working tree. A CLI session logged in with production rights (`az`, `aws`, `kubectl` contexts) counts as reachable unless the agent configuration asks before commands that use it.

evidence.detail: mise run release starts a production release

results.fix: In .claude/settings.json, put `gh workflow run`, `mise run release`, `git push --force`, `docker push`/`podman push` under ask.

results.name: Agent Change Traceability
results.why: Agent changes nobody can recognise can be neither reviewed with care nor evaluated.
results.passes_when: a documented rule makes agent changes recognisable (a co-author trailer, a pull request label, a bot account, a field in the pull request template), and the recent history follows it. Traces of agents alone are `agentic_development`.

evidence.detail: no trailers in the last 200 commits

results.fix: Pick a marking rule (Co-Authored-By trailer or an `agent` PR label), write it in the agent guide and follow it.

results.name: Dependency Update Automation
results.why: Keeps the dependencies the agent reasons about current.
results.passes_when: dependency updates are automated.

evidence.detail: actions, npm and docker; gomod for remake/ missing

results.name: Automated Security Review
results.why: Vulnerabilities an agent introduces are caught before release.
results.passes_when: a security scanner runs on changes.
results.fix: Enable CodeQL default setup (Go, JavaScript, Actions) on the repository.

results.name: License Compliance
results.why: An agent adds dependencies without asking; a license check stops one the project may not use before it ships.
results.passes_when: the allowed licenses are written down and CI checks the dependencies against them. An SBOM alone does not count.
results.fix: Write the allowed licenses down and add go-licenses (or dependency-review-action with allow-licenses) to CI.

results.name: Log Scrubbing
results.why: Agent-written log lines stay free of secrets and personal data.
results.passes_when: a configured redaction list or masking filter covers tokens, credentials, and personal data. Masking a single field name does not count.
results.fix: Add a ReplaceAttr to the slog handler that redacts tokens and request bodies; today the server logs save names and errors only.

results.name: PII Handling
results.why: Tells the agent which data is sensitive.
results.passes_when: personal data is explicitly marked and handled by rules.

results.name: Secret Scanning
results.why: A leaked credential is stopped before it leaves the machine.
results.passes_when: secret scanning or push protection is active.
results.fix: Enable secret scanning and push protection in the repository settings (free for public repos).

results.name: DAST Scanning
results.why: Finds runtime vulnerabilities static checks miss.
results.passes_when: running endpoints are scanned dynamically.
results.fix: Run a ZAP baseline scan against the WASM image in CI (it is already started for the smoke test).

results.name: Privacy Compliance
results.why: Written down, these are rules the agent can follow; it cannot infer them from the code.
results.passes_when: privacy and compliance controls are documented: what is collected, why, how long it is kept.

results.name: Backlog Health
results.why: A healthy backlog is a queue of work an agent can pick up.
results.passes_when: in a sample of up to 30 open issues, at least two thirds carry a label and a description of the expected outcome.
results.fix: Track planned work (remake screens still to port, known deviations) as labelled GitHub issues with expected outcomes.

results.name: Issue Labeling System
results.why: Labels let the agent filter and prioritise.
results.passes_when: labels follow a consistent taxonomy, ideally defined as code, and a label or a written definition of ready marks the issues an agent can take on: small, clearly bounded, and checkable.

evidence.detail: GitHub default labels plus Dependabot labels; no definition of ready

results.fix: Define labels as code (labels.yml with a sync action) including one for agent-sized issues, e.g. `agent-ready`.

results.name: Issue Templates
results.why: Well-formed issues are well-formed agent tasks.
results.passes_when: templates exist for the common request types.
results.fix: Add bug and feature templates under .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/.

results.name: PR Templates
results.why: Agent PRs get a consistent shape with test evidence.
results.passes_when: a pull/merge request template exists, or a committed skill or command for working on this repo writes pull request descriptions in a fixed shape.
results.fix: Add .github/pull_request_template.md asking for summary, checks run, screenshots for screen changes.

results.name: Error-to-Insight Pipeline
results.why: Production signals become agent tasks.
results.passes_when: production errors automatically become tracked issues.
results.fix: Have the health check or an error tracker open a GitHub issue on repeated failures, or waive.

results.name: Product Analytics Instrumentation
results.why: Real usage lets changes be prioritised by impact.
results.passes_when: product analytics are instrumented.
results.fix: Count game starts and saves in the WASM server (privacy-friendly, no personal data), or waive for a hobby project.

questions.question: Does the code follow one style throughout with no legacy patterns to avoid?
Is there a record of which agent tools may be used here?

levels.name: Baseline
levels.summary: has formatter, linter, types, and unit tests running locally.
levels.agent_use: Analyse code, write docs and tests; a human reviews every change.

levels.name: Documented
levels.summary: writes its workflows down: agent guide, env template, schema, ownership.
levels.agent_use: Develop features with an agent, a human steering closely.

levels.name: Agent-ready
levels.summary: enforces its standards through automation: CI, hooks, tracing, releases.
levels.agent_use: Agents implement clearly bounded tickets on their own, reviewed by pull request.

levels.name: Optimized
levels.summary: measures its feedback loops: coverage gates, flaky tests, build times.
levels.agent_use: Several agents work in parallel in separate workspaces.

levels.name: Autonomous
levels.summary: feeds production signals back into the loop: canaries, rollback, error-to-issue.
levels.agent_use: Agents react to production signals: error, issue, fix pull request.

priorities.why: main takes direct pushes, so nothing the agent guide or CI asks for stops a change from landing.
The guide says to ask before `mise run release` and pushes, but no agent configuration makes the agent wait.
A public repo with an agent guide but no word on which agent use is welcome; one paragraph closes it.
Free for public repos and one setting; the cheapest step towards level 4.
CodeQL default setup covers Go, JavaScript and the workflows with one setting.

strengths.why: One mise task runs lint and every unit test, locally and in CI.
Both images are exercised end to end in CI and the remake's screens are driven headless.
Screen comparison with the original and decompilation lookups are written down as skills.
Glossary and ADRs give the game terms and the reasons behind embedding and the C random generator.
Releases tag and publish only once both images exist.
